title: The Pittsburgh Platform (1885)
hookLine: early American Reform set aside many rituals

cards: A room in Pittsburgh. A group of Reform rabbis around a table, papers everywhere, arguing late. They are not writing a prayer or a law code.
They are writing a platform: a short list of principles, the way a political party does, saying plainly what their movement holds and what it is ready to let go.
The document they finish is blunt enough that people are still quoting it, and still arguing with it. Some readers find it brave. Some find it a loss.
Today, you read a few of its lines for yourself.

teach.b: The Pittsburgh Platform. Its sentences are long and careful, so take them slowly. First, the law.

Speaking of the laws of Moses, the rabbis wrote that "we accept as binding only its moral laws, and maintain only such ceremonies as elevate and sanctify our lives, but reject all such as are not adapted to the views and habits of modern civilization."
The moral laws stay binding. Ceremonies stay too, if they lift a life. What goes is what, in their view, no longer fit.
The platform named the laws about diet, priestly purity and dress as belonging to another age, and said keeping them could get in the way of spiritual life now.
So kosher kitchens and much else were set aside as obligations. Third, the people.

teach.h: A RELIGIOUS COMMUNITY, NOT A NATION.
teach.b: "We consider ourselves no longer a nation, but a religious community," it said, expecting no return to the land and no restored sacrificial worship. Fourth, justice.
The platform closed by calling it a duty to help solve the problems of society on the basis of justice and righteousness.

teach.h: SUCH CEREMONIES AS ELEVATE AND SANCTIFY.
teach.b: Hold all four together and you see the shape of early American Reform: ethics and reason in the middle, much of ritual at the edge. Some Jews at the time welcomed it.
Others were deeply troubled by it, and the arguments it started helped draw the lines between the movements. Tomorrow, what later Reform did with it.

how: Reform Jews and historians read the Pittsburgh Platform as an early statement of American Reform principles; Reform congregations today often study it alongside later statements of the movement.

practice: Bring to mind something you once said with total confidence, about yourself, your family, or what matters, and hear it in your old voice.
Then ask what you'd say about it now: what stayed exactly the same, what you dropped, what you might want back. Don't scold the old voice; it was doing its best with what it knew.
